text.0: The AUTO MPG dataset was taken from the StatLib library maintained at Carnegie Mellon University. The dataset was used at the 1983 American Statistical Association Exposition.
text.1:
The term "Auto MPG" refers to miles per gallon, a unit of fuel efficiency measurement commonly used in the United States. This measure indicates how many miles a vehicle can travel on one gallon of fuel. However, "Auto MPG" is an English term and there is no direct translation in Spanish.

In Spanish, terms such as "consumo de combustible" or "rendimiento de combustible" are often used to refer to the fuel efficiency of a car. These terms indicate how many kilometres or miles a vehicle can travel on one litre or gallon of fuel, respectively.

It is important to note that different countries use different units of measurement for fuel consumption. For example, in some places the litre per 100 kilometres travelled (L/100 km) is used to indicate fuel efficiency.

intro.0:
Bar graphs are a visual representation that shows the comparison of different categories or groups using rectangular bars.
This type of graph uses the length or height of bars to represent the magnitude or quantity of a specific variable.
intro.1:
In a bar graph, the horizontal axis represents the categories or groups, while the vertical axis shows the magnitude or frequency of the variable being analyzed.
Each category has an individual bar, and the length or height of the bar is proportional to the corresponding value or quantity.
The bars can be horizontal or vertical, depending on the orientation of the chart.
intro.2: Bar charts have several notable features and applications:

list.0:
Category Comparison: Bar charts are ideal for visually comparing different categories or groups.
By looking at the bars, it is possible to quickly identify differences in magnitude or quantity between categories.
list.1:
Representation of categorical or discrete data: Bar graphs are suitable for representing categorical or discrete variables.
Each bar represents a specific category and the height or length of the bar shows the magnitude or quantity associated with that category.
list.2:
Category Sorting: Categories in a bar chart can be sorted based on different criteria, such as alphabetical order, order of magnitude, or any other logical order.
This allows specific patterns or trends to be highlighted between categories.
list.3:
Displaying frequencies or percentages: Bar graphs are also used to represent frequencies or percentages.
In this case, the height or length of the bars represents the proportion or percentage corresponding to each category.
list.4:
Effective presentation: Bar charts are an effective tool for presenting information in a clear and concise manner.
Their simple structure and ability to highlight differences between categories make them widely used in reports, presentations, and documents.
list.5:
Bar charts are an effective way to visualize and compare categories or groups based on their magnitude or quantity.
They are ideal for representing categorical or discrete data and allow for effective presentation of information.
Their simplicity and ability to highlight differences make them a commonly used tool in data analysis and communication.

end.0:
Bar charts are an effective way to visualize and compare categories or groups based on their magnitude or quantity.
They are ideal for representing categorical or discrete data and allow for effective presentation of information.
Their simplicity and ability to highlight differences make them a commonly used tool in data analysis and communication.

intro.0:
Box plots, also known as box-and-whisker plots or boxplots, are a visual representation used to show the distribution and statistical summaries of a set of numerical data.
This type of chart is based on a rectangle that represents the interquartile range (IQR), where the center line indicates the median and the extended lines, known as whiskers, represent the range of
values beyond the IQR.
intro.1:
In a box chart, the rectangle is drawn vertically or horizontally, and is delimited by two lines, one at the bottom and one at the top.
The line in the middle of the rectangle represents the median, which is the value that divides the ordered data into two equal parts.
The whiskers extend from the edges of the rectangle toward the extreme values, with a length determined by the variability of the data.
intro.2: Box charts have several notable features and applications:

list.0:
Statistical summary: Box charts provide a visual summary of the key statistics of a data set.
In addition to the median, you can also display quartiles (Q1 and Q3), which divide the data into four equal parts, and outliers, which are displayed as dots or asterisks outside the whiskers.
list.1:
Identification of asymmetries and outliers: By observing a Box type chart, it is possible to identify asymmetries in the distribution of the data.
If the whiskers are not the same length, it may indicate an asymmetry towards one of the ends.
Additionally, outliers outside the whiskers can be easily highlighted.
list.2:
Comparison between groups or categories: Box charts are also used to compare the distribution of data between different groups or categories.
By overlaying multiple boxplots on the same graph, it is possible to visualize differences in medians, interquartile ranges, and the presence of outliers between groups.
list.3:
Detect biases and distributions: Box graphs allow you to visually identify whether the data distribution is symmetrical or skewed towards one extreme.
If the center line of the rectangle is not in the middle, it may indicate a bias towards the opposite direction.
list.4:
Visualization of dispersions: In addition to providing information about the central position and variability of the data, box charts also allow you to visualize the dispersion and variability of the data in a single graph.
This can be useful to get a quick idea of the overall distribution and variability of the data.

end.0:
Box plots are a useful tool for visualizing the distribution, statistical summaries, and variability of a numerical data set.
They allow you to identify asymmetries, outliers and compare distributions between groups.
Their concise and effective visual representation makes them a commonly used tool in data analysis and communication.

intro.0:
Histogram graphs are a visual representation used to show the distribution of numerical or continuous data.
This type of graph is based on a set of adjacent rectangular bars, where the width of each bar represents a range of values and the height of the bar indicates the frequency or number of observations within that range.
interval.
intro.1:
In a histogram-type graph, the horizontal axis is used to represent the range of values of the variable under study, divided into intervals or bins.
The vertical axis represents the frequency or number of observations in each interval.
The height of each bar shows how many observations fall within that specific interval.
intro.2: Histogram-type charts have several notable features and applications:

list.0:
Viewing distributions: Histograms allow you to view the shape and distribution of numerical data.
They can show whether the data follows a symmetric, skewed, multimodal, or uniform distribution.
list.1:
Viewing distributions: Histograms allow you to view the shape and distribution of numerical data.
They can show whether the data follows a symmetric, skewed, multimodal, or uniform distribution.
list.2:
Trend and pattern analysis: Histograms can reveal patterns and trends in data.
For example, a distribution skewed left or right indicates asymmetry in the data, while a normal distribution shows approximate symmetry.
list.3:
Comparison of groups or categories: Histograms can also be used to compare the distribution of data between different groups or categories.
By overlaying multiple histograms on the same graph, it is possible to visualize the differences and similarities between groups.
list.4:
Density Estimation: In addition to showing absolute frequency, histograms can also provide a visual estimate of the probability density of the data.
By normalizing the heights of the bars, it is possible to obtain a relative representation of the probability of occurrence of the values in each interval.

end.0:
Histogram-type graphs are a useful tool for visualizing the distribution and patterns of numerical data.
They allow you to identify outliers, analyze trends and compare distributions between groups.
Their clear and concise visual representation makes them an effective tool for communicating information about data distribution in an understandable way.

intro.0:
Line graphs, also known as series graphs or trend graphs, are a visual representation that shows the relationship and evolution of data over time or a continuous variable.
These graphs are constructed by plotting data points in a Cartesian coordinate system, where each point represents a measurement or a specific value of the variable on the vertical axis as a function of time or the variable.
independent on the horizontal axis.
intro.1:
In a line graph, data points are connected by straight lines, creating a series of connected points.
These lines allow you to visualize the trajectory and pattern of change of the data over time or of the independent variable.
The slope of the line can indicate an increasing or decreasing trend, while variations in the direction and shape of the line can reveal additional patterns in the data.
intro.2: Line type charts have several notable features and applications:

list.0:
Representation of trends: Line-type graphs are especially useful for showing trends and changes over time.
They can reveal patterns of growth, decline, or fluctuation in data as they occur over time.
list.1:
Identification of changes and variations: By observing a line graph, it is possible to identify abrupt changes or variations in the data.
These changes may indicate significant events or factors that influence the measured variable.
list.2:
Comparing Multiple Series: Line charts also allow you to compare multiple data series on a single chart.
This is useful for analyzing and visualizing the relationship between different variables as they evolve over time.
list.3:
Seasonality and cycle analysis: If the data exhibits seasonal or cyclical patterns, line graphs can help identify and analyze these patterns.
This can be useful in fields such as economics, meteorology, and sales analysis, where there are recurring fluctuations in data.
list.4:
Forecasting and projection: Line type charts are also used to make forecasts and projections based on historical data.
By looking at past trends, it is possible to infer and predict how data will behave in the future.

end.0:
"Line graphs are a valuable tool for visualizing and analysing the relationship and evolution of data over time or a continuous variable.
They allow you to identify trends, changes and patterns in the data, as well as make comparisons and forecasts.
Their clear and concise visual representation makes them an effective tool for communicating complex information in an understandable way."

intro.0:
Pie or pie charts are a visual representation that shows the proportion of different categories or parts in relation to the whole.
These graphs are based on a circle divided into sectors, where each sector represents a specific category and its relative size reflects the proportion that category represents in the data set.
intro.1:
In a pie chart, the full circle represents 100% or the total data.
Each sector is shown as a portion of the circle and is labeled with the name or label corresponding to the category it represents.
The sector angle measure is proportional to the proportion that category has in the data set.
intro.2: Pie charts have several notable features and applications:

list.0:
Representation of proportions: Pie charts are ideal for representing proportions and percentages.
They allow you to quickly visualize the relative contribution of each category in the total data set.
list.1:
Identifying Dominant Categories: The relative sizes of the slices in the pie chart help to easily identify the dominant or most significant categories.
The largest sectors indicate the categories that have a greater proportion or contribution in relation to the others.
list.2:
Comparison between categories: While pie charts are useful for showing the proportions of categories, they can be limited in making accurate comparisons between them.
This is because human perception can have difficulty accurately evaluating differences in angle or sector sizes.
However, the relative comparison between sector sizes can still provide general information about the proportions between categories.
list.3:
Representing Categorical Data: Pie charts are especially useful for representing categorical data, where the categories are mutually exclusive and have no inherent order.
For example, they can be used to show the percentage distribution of income across different expense categories.
list.4:
"Improving Visual Presentation: Pie charts are commonly used in presentations and documents to communicate information in a visually appealing and easily understandable way.
The circular shape and colors used can quickly capture attention and highlight the proportional relationships between categories."

end.0:
Pie charts are an effective tool for representing proportions and percentages of categories in a data set.
They allow the dominant categories to be identified and provide an attractive visual presentation.
However, it is important to note its limitations in terms of accurate comparison between categories and its focus on categorical data.

intro.0:
A scatter plot, also known as a dot plot or scatter plot in English, is a visual representation that uses Cartesian coordinates to show the relationship between two variables.
In this type of graph, data is represented as individual points in two-dimensional space, where each point represents a pair of values corresponding to the two variables.
intro.1:
In a scatter plot, the horizontal axis is usually assigned to the independent variable, while the vertical axis is assigned to the dependent variable.
Each point on the graph represents an individual observation and its position on the graph is determined by the values it has for both variables.
The relative location of the points on the graph reveals patterns and relationships between the two variables.
intro.2: Scatter charts have several notable applications and features:

list.0:
Relationship between variables: Scatter graphs allow you to analyze the relationship between two variables.
They can show whether there is a positive correlation (the points tend to cluster in an upward direction), a negative correlation (the points tend to cluster in a downward direction), or a lack of correlation (the points do not show a definite pattern).
list.1:
Identifying trends: A scatter plot can reveal trends or patterns in the data.
By looking at the general direction of the points, it is possible to identify whether there is a linear, nonlinear, or even a curvilinear relationship between the variables.
list.2:
Outlier Detection: Scatter plots can help identify outliers or extremes in data.
These points stand out and are far from the main grouping, suggesting unusual or exceptional observations that may require additional analysis.
list.3:
Analysis of clusters or groups: If the points in the scatter plot group together or form distinct patterns, this may indicate the presence of clusters or groups.
This can be useful in data segmentation or classification analysis.
list.4:
Visualization of multi-dimensional data: If additional colors or point sizes are used, scatter plots can also represent additional information in a two-dimensional space.
This allows you to view multi-dimensional data in a more intuitive way.

end.0:
Scatter plots are a powerful tool for exploring and visualizing the relationship between two variables.
They allow you to identify patterns, trends and outliers in the data, and are useful in various applications, such as correlation analysis, cluster detection and visualization of multi-dimensional data.

time-series-plots.title: Time Series Plots

intro.0:
A time series chart is a visual representation of data that is collected and recorded at regular intervals over time.
These charts are widely used in various disciplines, such as economics, finance, meteorology, engineering, and many others, to analyze and understand how data changes over time.
intro.1:
The horizontal axis of the graph represents time, while the vertical axis shows the data values being observed or recorded.
Data points are connected with lines, allowing patterns and trends to be identified over time.
intro.2: Time series charts offer several advantages and practical applications:

list.0:
Trend Analysis: Time series graphs allow you to identify and analyze long-term trends in data.
This can be useful for predicting how data will behave in the future and making informed decisions.
list.1:
Identifying seasonal patterns: In many data sets, there are seasonal patterns that repeat regularly over time, such as holiday sales or seasonal fluctuations in agricultural production.
Time series charts help identify these seasonal patterns and understand their impact on the data.
list.2:
Detection of changes and anomalies: By observing a time series graph, it is possible to identify abrupt changes or anomalies in the data.
These changes may indicate important or unusual events that require further investigation and analysis.
list.3:
Modeling and forecasting: Time series graphs are a fundamental tool for developing models and forecasts.
By looking at past patterns, it is possible to build mathematical or statistical models that capture relationships and allow predictions about the future.
list.4:
Comparative Analysis: Time series charts are also used to compare different sets of data that are collected during the same time period.
This can help identify differences, similarities and relationships between the observed variables.

end.0:
Time series charts are an essential tool for analyzing and understanding how data changes over time.
They provide valuable information on trends, seasonal patterns, changes and forecasts, enabling informed decisions and comparative analysis.

intro.0:
A violin plot is a visual representation that combines features of a box-and-whisker plot with a probability density function.
This type of chart provides a detailed view of the distribution of the data and allows you to compare multiple groups or categories in a single chart.
intro.1:
The appearance of a violin chart resembles the shape of a violin, hence its name.
It has a center line that represents the median of the data and two shaded areas on either side that represent the probability density distribution.
These shaded areas of symmetry along the center line to reflect the symmetry or asymmetry of the data.
intro.2:
The violin plot shape provides information about the distribution of the data.
For example, a wider violin plot in a particular section indicates a higher density of data in that area, while a narrower section indicates a lower density.
Additionally, violin charts can have multiple violins grouped or overlapping to allow visual comparison of different groups or categories.
intro.3: Violin charts have several practical applications:

list.0:
Comparing Distributions: Violin plots allow you to compare data distributions between different groups or categories.
This is useful for identifying differences or similarities in the shape, dispersion, and trends of the data.
list.1:
Identifying Outliers: Violin plots provide visual information about the presence of outliers or extremes in the data.
These values are represented as points outside the shaded areas and may indicate unusual observations that may require additional analysis.
list.2:
Probability Density Visualization: Violin plots also provide a graphical representation of the probability density of the data.
This allows areas of high or low density, as well as possible biases or asymmetries in the distribution, to be easily identified.
list.3:
Effective data communication: Violin charts are an effective way to communicate complex information about the distribution of data in a visually appealing way.
They can summarize information concisely and help convey important patterns and features to a non-technical audience.

end.0:
Violin plots are a useful tool for visualizing and comparing data distributions.
They allow you to analyze the shape, dispersion, symmetry and presence of outliers in the data, and are especially useful when comparison between multiple groups or categories is required.
Their attractive and concise graphical representation makes them an effective tool for communicating complex information in an understandable way.

tabular-classification.title: Tabular classification
tabular-classification.text-1: Tabular classification is a type of supervised learning in which a set of labelled data is used to train a machine learning model, so that the model can predict the class of new data examples not used in training. In tabular classification, input and output data are represented in the form of a table with rows and columns, where each row represents an instance or example of the data, and each column represents a characteristic or attribute of the data.
tabular-classification.text-2: For example, if you want to predict whether a bank of a bank is solvent or not, the characteristics or attributes that can be used are: income, debts, credit history, age, etc. In the tabular classification, each instance or example of the data set will have values for each of these characteristics and a label (class) that indicates whether the client is solvent or not.
tabular-classification.text-3: Once you have a set of data labeled, a machine learning algorithm is used to train a model that can predict the label of new data sets. This model can be used to perform precise and fast predictions on new data instances.
tabular-classification.text-4: Tabular classification is a very useful technique to solve classification problems in a wide variety of fields, such as medicine, electronic commerce, banking, safety and many others.

text.0: Regression is a statistical analysis method used in machine learning to model the linear relationship between an independent variable and a dependent variable, seeking to find the best straight line that fits the data and allows predictions to be made.
text.1: In regression, data is usually represented as scattered points on a Cartesian plane, where the independent variable is placed on the + b) that minimizes the distance between this line and the data points. Once this equation has been obtained, it can be used to make predictions about future values of the dependent variable based on the values of the independent variable.
text.2: For example, if we are analyzing the relationship between the amount of advertising on a website and the sales of a product, the amount of advertising would be the independent variable, and the sales of the product would be the dependent variable. Regression would help us determine if there is a linear relationship between advertising spend and sales, and if so, it would allow us to predict future sales based on advertising spend.
text.3: Regression is a powerful tool in data analysis and is used in a variety of fields, including economics, social science, medical research, and many other disciplines to understand and predict relationships between variables.

object-identification.title: Object identification
object-identification.text-1: Object identification in neural networks is a technique used in the field of machine learning and computer vision to detect and recognize objects in images or videos. It is an important task in image analysis and is used in applications such as face recognition, real-time object tracking, object classification in medical images, and object detection in autonomous vehicles.
object-identification.text-2: The neural networks used for the identification of objects are deep learning models that are trained in data sets labeled. The training process implies providing the neurons network for a large number of images tagged, and adjusting the weights of connections between neurons so that the network can identify objects in new images with high precision.
object-identification.text-3: Once the neural network has been trained, it is used to identify objects in new images. The network examines the image and, by processing multiple layers, extracts important characteristics that are used to identify objects of interest. Then, the network uses these characteristics to assign a label to each object detected in the image.
object-identification.text-4: In summary, object identification in neural networks is an important technique in computer vision and machine learning that is used to detect and recognize objects in images and videos. It is based on the use of deep neural networks trained on labeled data sets to identify and classify objects in new images with high accuracy.

image-classification.title: Image classification
image-classification.text-1: Image classification is a technique used in neural networks to classify images into different categories or labels. The goal of an image classifier is to take an input image and predict which class it belongs to, based on a set of predefined categories or labels.
image-classification.text-2: In deep learning, image classifiers are based on convolutional neural networks (CNN), which are a specialized architecture to process images. These neural networks have multiple layers and convolution operations that allow them to extract important characteristics from the images, such as edges, shapes and textures.
image-classification.text-3: To train an image classifier, a set of labeled data is used that contains images and their respective class labels. Then, the neural network is trained using this dataset to learn to identify patterns in the images and associate them with the corresponding class labels.
image-classification.text-4: Once the neural network has been trained, it can be used to classify new images in different categories. The image classifier examines the input image and processes it through the neural network to extract important characteristics and predict what class the image belongs.
image-classification.text-5: In short, image classification in neural networks is a technique that uses convolutional neural networks to classify images into different categories or labels. It is based on using a set of labeled data to train the neural network and extracting important features from the images to predict which class a new input image belongs to.

activation-functions.title: Activation functions
activation-functions.text-1: An activation function is a mathematical function used in an artificial neural network to determine the output of a neuron or a set of neurons based on the entry received. The activation function introduces non -linearity in the neural network, allowing the network to learn more complex patterns in the input data. Common examples of activation functions are:

linear.title: Linear
linear.description: Returns the input unchanged (the identity). It is the activation of the output layer in regression, where the network must be able to output any number.

characteristics.0: It does not limit the output range.
characteristics.1: A network with only linear layers is equivalent to a single linear layer: it cannot learn non-linear relationships.

softmax.title: Softmax
softmax.description: Transforms outputs to a representation in the form of probabilities, so that the sum of all probabilities gives 1

characteristics.2: Used to normalize multi class type

sigmoid.title: Sigmoid
sigmoid.description: The sigmoid function transforms the input values into a range between 0 and 1. is commonly used in neural networks for binary classification problems.

characteristics.1: Useful in the output layer of binary classifiers.
characteristics.2: You can suffer the problem of fading of the gradient in deep networks.

hard-sigmoid.title: Hard Sigmoid
hard-sigmoid.description: Hard Sigmoid is a simplified version of the sigmoid function used for computational efficiency.

characteristics.0: It is faster to calculate than sigmoid.
characteristics.1: Less soft in the transition between 0 and 1.

relu.title: ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit)
relu.description: The ReLU function is simple and effective when returning zero for negative values and maintaining positive values without changes

relu6.title: ReLU 6
relu6.description: Similar to ReLU, but with a higher limitation of 6 for positive values, which can help avoid the explosion of gradients.

characteristics.1: Useful in networks with unstable gradients.

leaky-relu.title: LeakyReLU
leaky-relu.description: Leaky ReLU is a ReLU variant that allows a small fraction of negative values to pass through the function.

characteristics.0: Mitigate the death problem of neurons compared to reluct.
characteristics.1: It helps maintain information in negative gradients.

elu.title: ELU (Exponential Linear Unit)
elu.description: ELU is a function that resembles ReLU in positive values, but also has a defined gradient for negative values.

characteristics.0: Reduce the problem of fading of the gradient.
characteristics.1: It helps keep more neurons active.

tanh.title: Tanh (hyperbolic tangent)
tanh.description: The hyperbolic tangent function transforms the input values into a range [-1, 1].

characteristics.2: Suffers from fading of the gradient in deep networks.

soft-plus.title: SoftPlus
soft-plus.description: SoftPlus is a soft function that is often used as a soft alternative to reluct.

characteristics.1: It can be useful in generative and regression networks.

mish.title: Mish
mish.description: Mish is a relatively new activation function that combines characteristics of other functions such as hyperbolic tangent and sigmoid function.

characteristics.0: Softness and derivability in its entire range.
characteristics.1: It provides better performance in some applications.

selu.title: SELU (Scaled Exponential Linear Unit)
selu.description: SELU is a function that benefits from specific standardization and can help maintain network stability.

characteristics.0: Autocalibration: stable statistical propagates through the layers.
characteristics.1: It can be useful in networks with self-chire architecture.

units.title: Layer Neurons
units.description: These are the individual units or nodes in a specific layer of the network. Each neuron receives inputs, performs computations and produces an output that is transmitted to the next layer. The number of neurons in a layer can vary and is usually a hyperparameter of the model. The choice of the number of neurons in a layer affects the model's ability to learn representations of the data.

activation-function.title: Layer Activation Function
activation-function.description: At each neuron in a layer of a neural network, an activation function is applied to introduce non-linearity into the model. The activation function determines the output of the neuron as a function of its input and associated weights.

learning-rate.title: Learning Rate
learning-rate.description: The learning rate is a crucial hyperparameter in machine learning algorithms and neural networks. It determines how much the model weights must be updated at each iteration during the training process. A high learning rate can lead to fast convergence, but can result in instability, while a low rate can lead to slow convergence or get stuck in local minima.

number-or-epochs.title: Number of Epochs
number-or-epochs.description: Epochs refer to the number of times the entire training data set has been passed through the model during the training process. A higher number of epochs generally allows the model to fit the data better, but can also lead to overfitting if a certain limit is exceeded.

test-size.title: Test Size
test-size.description: The amount of data that is set aside to evaluate the performance of the model after training. The test set is used to measure the accuracy and overall performance of the model on unseen data.

optimizer.title: Optimizer
optimizer.description: The optimizer is an algorithm that adjusts the parameters of a machine learning model during training. Its goal is to minimize the loss function by updating the model weights efficiently. Examples of common optimizers include Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), Adam and RMSprop.

loss-function.title: Loss Function
loss-function.description: The loss function is a measure that quantifies how well the model is performing in its predictions. It helps to calculate the difference between the model's predictions and the actual values of the data set. The goal of training is to minimize this function, as a low loss value indicates that the model is a better fit to the data.

metric-function.title: Metric Function
metric-function.description: Unlike the loss function, which is used to optimise the model during training, metric functions are used to evaluate the performance of the model after training. These metrics provide information on accuracy, recall, precision, F1-score, etc., and help to understand how the model performs on specific tasks.

optimization-functions.title: Optimization functions
optimization-functions.text-1: An optimization function is a mathematical technique used to minimize or maximize an objective function. In the context of machine learning, the target functions are usually error functions that measure the discrepancy between the neural network output and the desired output values for a given training dataset.
optimization-functions.text-2: The optimization function adjusts the parameters of the neural network to minimize the objective function and, therefore, improve its ability to make precise predictions in new entry data. Common examples of optimization functions are the descent of the stochastic gradient and the Adam algorithm.

sgd.references:
Stochastic gradient descent
 (Autonomous Technological Institute of Mexico, 2017)
sgd.description:
The descent of the gradient is an algorithm that estimates where a function generates its lower values. In the event that the machine learning model is large -scale this calculation can be very expensive.
                          Because of this, the descent of the stochastic gradient that uses a constant and therefore the number of gradients to be calculated arises.

momentum.description: It is a variation of the previous function. Define a value that accelerates the descent of the gradient if the gradient sign is the same during different times.

adagrad.description: Enter a variation in the concept of learning rate. This scale and adapts this value for each weight with respect to the accumulated gradient in each iteration.

adadelta.description: It is a variation of AdaGrad in which the calculation of the learning rate of each weight is restricted to a fixed size window of the last n gradients instead of doing so with the accumulated gradient of each iteration.

rmsprop.references:
Middle quadratic root propagation
 (Root Mean Square Propagation)
 (Velasco, 2020)
rmsprop.description: This algorithm maintains a different training factor for each dimension, but the scaling of the training factor is done by dividing it by the average of the exponential decline of the square of the gradients.

adam.references:
Adaptive estimation of the mo
 (Adaptive Moment Estimation)
 (Velasco, 2020)
adam.description: It is a combination of AdaGrad and RMSProp . A parameter training factor is maintained and RMSProp is calculated, in addition each training factor is affected by the momentum of the gradient.

adamax.description: It combines momentum and adaptive learning techniques to accelerate convergence during neural network training. It automatically adjusts the learning rate and uses gradient scaling to avoid divergence issues.

text.0: In machine learning, a loss function (also called cost function) is a measure that quantifies the discrepancy between the predicted exit by a model and the real or desired output. In other words, the loss function measures how well the model conforms to training data.
text.1: The objective of a machine learning algorithm is to minimize the loss function, which means finding the model set of the model that best suits training data. Therefore, the choice of loss function is very important, since it can affect the model ability to correctly learn patterns in the data and make precise predictions in new data.
text.2: These are the loss functions you can choose in Nets4Learning, grouped by the type of task where they make sense:

categoricalCrossentropy.description: Measures the difference between the probabilities predicted by the model and the true class (one-hot encoded). It is the usual loss for multi-class classification with a softmax output.

binaryCrossentropy.description: Cross-entropy for two classes, or for several independent labels, with a sigmoid output.

kullbackLeiblerDivergence.description: Measures how far the predicted probability distribution is from the true one. Used when the model output is a distribution.

hinge.description: Penalises predictions that do not exceed a margin with respect to the correct class. It comes from support vector machines and expects -1 and 1 labels.

squaredHinge.description: Like the hinge loss, but squared: large errors are penalised more.

categoricalHinge.description: Hinge loss for several classes: compares the score of the correct class with that of the best wrong class.

meanSquaredError.description: Mean of the squared differences between the true and the predicted value. It penalises large errors heavily; it is the usual loss for regression.

meanAbsoluteError.description: Mean of the absolute differences between the true and the predicted value. It is less affected by outliers than the squared error.

meanAbsolutePercentageError.description: Mean absolute error expressed as a percentage of the true value. Useful to compare errors across different magnitudes, but true values cannot be zero.

meanSquaredLogarithmicError.description: Mean squared error on the logarithm of the values: it measures the relative error and penalises errors on large values less.

logcosh.description: Logarithm of the hyperbolic cosine of the error: it behaves like the squared error for small errors and like the absolute error for large ones.

poisson.description: Meant for predicting counts (non-negative integers), such as the number of visits or events.

cosineProximity.description: Compares the direction of the true and the predicted vectors (the angle between them), regardless of their size.

metric-functions.title: Metric functions
metric-functions.text-1: They are used to evaluate the performance of the neural network model in a test data set. The metric function takes the predictions made by the model and compare them with the real values of the test data to determine the precision of the model.
metric-functions.text-2: There are different types of metric functions that can be used in a neural network, depending on the type of problem that is being addressed. For example, for a problem of binary classification, precision (Accuracy) could be used as metric, while for a regression problem the average quadratic error could be used (Mean Squared Error).
metric-functions.text-3: In summary, a metric function is an important tool to assess the ability of a neural network to perform precise predictions in a test dataset and to help adjust the model parameters to improve its performance.
metric-functions.text-4: We mainly use the accuracy function. In multi-label classification, this function calculates subset precision: the predicted set of labels for a sample must exactly match the corresponding set of labels in y

BinaryAccuracy.description: Calculate the frequency with which the predictions coincide with binary labels.

BinaryCrossentropy.description: It is the negative average of the logarithm of the predicted chances that have been corrected.

CategoricalAccuracy.description: Calculate the frequency with which the predictions coincide with the ONE-Hot labels.

CategoricalCrossentropy.description: Calculate the crossed entropy metric between labels and predictions.

CosineProximity.description: Calculate between labels and predictions the proximity cosine. Normally negative values are obtained.

MeanAbsoluteError.description: In statistics, it is a measure of the difference between two continuous variables, applied to machine learning models These variables are labels and predictions.

MeanAbsolutePercentageError.description: In the same way that Mean absolute error calculates the difference between labels and predictions, but in this case with a percentage.

MeanSquaredError.description: Determine the average quadratic error between labels and predictions.

confusion.title: Confusion matrix metrics
confusion.description: They are computed from the hits and misses of each class in the confusion matrix: how many positive predictions are correct (precision), how many real positives are found (recall or sensitivity), the harmonic mean of both (F1) and how many real negatives are recognised (specificity).

intro.title: Car classification
intro.content: On this page, a neural network that has already been trained decides whether a car is acceptable from six features: the buying price, the maintenance, the doors, the seats, the luggage boot and the safety. I will explain what each thing is, step by step. You can move on with Next, go back, mute the voice or let the guide move on by itself.

model.title: The model
model.content: This is the model card. It tells you where the data comes from, the Car Evaluation data set from the UCI repository, which features the network receives and which classes it can predict.

model-summary.title: Model summary
model-summary.content: This button opens the summary of the network: its layers, how many neurons each one has and how many parameters, which are the weights it adjusted during training.

dataset.title: The data set
dataset.content: These are the 1728 cars the network was trained with. Each row is a car and each column is one of its features. The last column, highlighted, is the class: what the network learned to predict.

dataset-processed.title: Processed data
dataset-processed.content: A neural network only works with numbers. In this tab you will see the same cars with every category turned into a number: for example, the four possible prices become numbers from 0 to 3. This is how the model receives them.

instances.title: Examples and rows
instances.content: With this selector you fill in the whole form at once. At the top are the examples, marked with a star, one for each class; below them, every row of the data set with its real class.

Buying.title: Buying price
Buying.content: How much it costs to buy the car: very high, high, medium or low.

Maint.title: Price of the maintenance
Maint.content: What it costs to keep the car running, with its services and repairs. It also goes from very high to low.

Doors.title: Number of doors
Doors.content: Two, three, four, or five or more. It is the feature with the least influence on the decision.

Persons.title: Capacity in persons
Persons.content: How many people fit: two, four or more. In this data, a car with only two seats is always unacceptable.

Lug_boot.title: Size of the luggage boot
Lug_boot.content: Small, medium or big. The bigger the boot, the more acceptable the car.

Safety.title: Safety
Safety.content: The estimated safety of the car: low, medium or high. It is the feature that weighs the most: with low safety, the car is always unacceptable.

vector.title: From words to numbers
vector.content: On the left are the values of the form and, on the right, the vector that goes into the network: the same six features turned into numbers with the encoding learned during training.

classify.title: Classify
classify.content: When you press this button, the network receives the vector, passes it through layer after layer and computes a probability for each class.

result.title: The result
result.content: Here you will see the probability of each class, and the highest one is the prediction. If you classify an example or a row without changing it, you will also see its real class, so you can check whether the network gets it right. This model only has three outputs: unacceptable, acceptable and very good. The class good has none, so it is never predicted.

explain.title: Explainability
explain.content: After classifying, here you can see why the network decided that. SHAP shares out the decision among the features: which ones push towards the class and which ones against it. The global importance does the same with many rows, to see which feature weighs the most in general.

end.title: Your turn
end.content: Try choosing an example, classify it, and then change the safety or the number of seats to see how the prediction changes. You can open this guide again whenever you like with the Guide button.

intro.title: Iris flower classification
intro.content: On this page, a neural network that has already been trained recognises the species of an iris flower from four measurements: the length and width of the sepal and of the petal. I will explain what each thing is, step by step. You can move on with Next, go back, mute the voice or let the guide move on by itself.

dataset.title: The data set
dataset.content: It is the famous Iris data set, which the statistician Ronald Fisher made known in 1936: 150 flowers, 50 of each species. Each row is a flower with its four measurements in centimetres, and the last column, highlighted, is its species.

sepal_length.title: Sepal length
sepal_length.content: The sepal is the green leaf that protects the flower before it opens. This box is its length, in centimetres.

sepal_width.title: Sepal width
sepal_width.content: The width of the sepal, in centimetres. It is the measurement that helps the least to tell the species apart.

petal_length.title: Petal length
petal_length.content: The length of the petal, in centimetres. Together with its width, it is the measurement that best separates the species: the setosa has much smaller petals than the other two.

petal_width.title: Petal width
petal_width.content: The width of the petal, in centimetres. In this data, a flower whose petal is less than one centimetre wide is always a setosa.

vector.title: From the data to the vector
vector.content: Here the four measurements are already numbers, so the vector that goes into the network is those same measurements, in the same order.

result.title: The result
result.content: Here you will see the probability of each species: setosa, versicolor and virginica. The highest one is the prediction. The setosa is easy to recognise; the other two look more alike, and that is where the network may hesitate.

end.title: Your turn
end.content: Choose the versicolor example, classify it and increase the length and width of the petal little by little: you will see the network start to hesitate and end up saying virginica. You can open this guide again whenever you like with the Guide button.

intro.title: Lymphography classification
intro.content: On this page, a neural network that has already been trained classifies the result of a lymphography, an imaging test of the lymphatic system, into four diagnoses: normal, metastases, malignant lymphoma or fibrosis. I will explain what each thing is, step by step. You can move on with Next, go back, mute the voice or let the guide move on by itself.

dataset.title: The data set
dataset.content: These are 148 patients from the Institute of Oncology of the University Medical Centre in Ljubljana. Each row is a patient and each column is something observed in their lymphography. The classes are very unbalanced: there are 81 cases of metastases and 61 of malignant lymphoma, but only 4 of fibrosis and 2 normal ones.

form.title: What the lymphography shows
form.content: The form has eighteen features. Some say whether the lymphatic vessels are normal, arched, deformed or displaced; others, whether there are blockages, bypasses or leaks of the contrast; and others describe the lymph nodes: how many there are, whether they have grown or shrunk, their shape and the defects and changes in their structure. They are medical terms: you do not need to understand them all to see how the prediction changes.

result.title: The result
result.content: Here you will see the probability of each diagnosis, and the highest one is the prediction. With so few cases of fibrosis and normal results, the network has mostly learned to tell metastases from malignant lymphoma.

end.title: Your turn
end.content: Choose an example of each diagnosis, classify it, and then look at the explainability to see which features weighed the most in each one. You can open this guide again whenever you like with the Guide button.

model.title: The model
model.content: This is the model card: where the data comes from, which variables the network receives and which one it predicts.

model-summary.title: Model summary
model-summary.content: This button opens the summary of the network: its layers, how many neurons each one has and how many parameters, which are the weights it adjusted during training.

dataset-select.title: Data set
dataset-select.content: Here you choose the data set. Each one has its own trained networks.

dataset.title: The data set
dataset.content: This is the data the network was trained with. Each row is an example and each column is a variable. The highlighted column is the target variable: the number the network learned to predict.

dataset-processed.title: Processed data
dataset-processed.content: In this tab you will see the same data as the model receives it, with the texts turned into numbers, and below it the statistical description of each column.

dataset-analysis.title: Analysis
dataset-analysis.content: This tab sums up the exploratory analysis of the data set: its size, the missing values, how the target variable is distributed and which variables are most related to it. It is a good place to understand the data before predicting.

instances.title: Rows of the data set
instances.content: With this selector you fill in the form with any row of the data set. Next to the row number you will see its real value, to compare it with the prediction afterwards.

models.title: Models
models.content: Here you choose one of the networks already trained for this data set.

form.title: The form
form.content: Here you write the values of the input variables, one box per variable. Under each one you will see its type and the range of values it takes in the data.

predict.title: Predict
predict.content: When you press this button, the network receives the values already encoded and scaled, passes them through layer after layer and returns a number: its prediction.

result.title: The result
result.content: Here you will see the predicted value. If you used a row of the data set without changing it, you will also see its real value and the error, the difference between the two. Below are the steps the data goes through before entering the network.

explain.title: Explainability
explain.content: After predicting, here you can see why the network gave that value. SHAP shares out the prediction among the variables: which ones raise it and which ones lower it compared with the average prediction. The global importance does the same with many rows, to see which variable weighs the most in general.

end.title: Your turn
end.content: Choose a row, predict its value and then change a variable to see how the prediction changes. You can open this guide again whenever you like with the Guide button.

intro.title: Fuel efficiency
intro.content: On this page, a neural network that has already been trained predicts how many miles a car travels on one gallon of fuel, from six facts about the car: the cylinders, the displacement, the horsepower, the weight, the acceleration and the model year. I will explain what each thing is, step by step. You can move on with Next, go back, mute the voice or let the guide move on by itself.

dataset-select.title: Data set
dataset-select.content: This model has a single data set, Auto MPG.

dataset.title: The data set
dataset.content: These are 396 cars from 1970 to 1982, from the Auto MPG data set. The highlighted column, mpg, is the miles per gallon: the higher it is, the less the car uses. In this data it goes from 9 to 46.

cylinders.title: Cylinders
cylinders.content: The number of cylinders of the engine, from three to eight. More cylinders usually mean more consumption.

displacement.title: Displacement
displacement.content: The total volume of the cylinders of the engine, in cubic inches. The bigger it is, the more fuel the car uses.

horsepower.title: Horsepower
horsepower.content: The power of the engine. More powerful cars usually travel fewer miles per gallon.

weight.title: Weight
weight.content: The weight of the car, in pounds. It is the variable most related to consumption: the heavier the car, the fewer miles it travels per gallon.

acceleration.title: Acceleration
acceleration.content: The seconds the car takes to go from 0 to 60 miles per hour. A higher number is a less sporty car, which usually uses less fuel.

model-year.title: Model year
model-year.content: The year the model came out, with two digits, from 70 to 82. The newer cars in this data set use less fuel, partly because of the fuel economy laws of those years.

result.title: The result
result.content: Here you will see the predicted consumption, in miles per gallon. If you used a row without changing it, you will also see the real value and the error. Below are the steps the data goes through before entering the network.

end.title: Your turn
end.content: Choose a car, predict its consumption and then raise its weight or horsepower: you will see the network predict fewer miles per gallon. You can open this guide again whenever you like with the Guide button.

intro.title: Student performance
intro.content: On this page, a neural network that has already been trained predicts the final grade of a secondary school student, from 0 to 20, from thirty facts about their school, family and social life. I will explain what each thing is, step by step. You can move on with Next, go back, mute the voice or let the guide move on by itself.

model.title: The model
model.content: This is the model card: where the data comes from, which variables the network receives and which one it predicts. The note about G1 and G2 that you will see in it refers to the original data: this version leaves them out on purpose, as I will explain later.

dataset-select.title: Data set
dataset-select.content: There are two data sets: maths students and Portuguese language students, from two secondary schools in Portugal. Each one has its own trained network.

dataset.title: The data set
dataset.content: Each row is a student: 395 in maths and 649 in Portuguese. The highlighted column, G3, is the final grade of the year, from 0 to 20. Two columns of the original data are missing here, G1 and G2, the grades of the first and second terms: they were removed on purpose.

form.title: The student data
form.content: The form has thirty variables: personal ones, such as age and sex; family ones, such as the education and job of the mother and father; school ones, such as study time, past failures and absences; and social ones, such as going out with friends or alcohol consumption. Past failures are what is most related to a low final grade. The term grades are not here: the next step explains why.

grades.title: What about the grades G1 and G2?
grades.content: G1 and G2 are the grades of the first and second terms, and they are very close to the final one: their correlation with G3 goes from 0.8 to 0.92. With them, the network would hardly have to learn anything, it would be enough to copy the grade of the second term. Without them, it has to predict the final grade only from the school, family and social life of the student. It is much harder, but also much more useful: it can be done before there are any grades, to help in time those who need it. That is why the networks on this page were trained without G1 and G2.

result.title: The result
result.content: Here you will see the predicted final grade, from 0 to 20. If you used a row without changing it, you will also see the real grade and the error. Since the network does not know the term grades, it is normal for it to be off by a few points: that is the price of being able to predict before there are any grades.

end.title: Your turn
end.content: Choose a student, predict their grade and then change the number of past failures or the study time to see how the prediction changes. You can open this guide again whenever you like with the Guide button.

intro.title: Wine quality
intro.content: On this page, a neural network that has already been trained predicts the quality of a Portuguese wine, the score given by wine tasters, from eleven chemical measurements. I will explain what each thing is, step by step. You can move on with Next, go back, mute the voice or let the guide move on by itself.

dataset-select.title: Data set
dataset-select.content: There are two data sets: red wine and white wine, from the vinho verde region. Each one has its own trained network.

dataset.title: The data set
dataset.content: Each row is a wine: 1599 reds and 4898 whites. The highlighted column, quality, is the tasters' score, from 0 to 10, although in this data it only goes from 3 to 9 and almost every wine has a 5 or a 6.

form.title: The wine measurements
form.content: The form has eleven chemical measurements: fixed and volatile acidity, citric acid, residual sugar, chlorides, free and total sulphur dioxide, density, pH, sulphates and alcohol. Alcohol is the one most related to quality: wines with more alcohol usually score better. In reds, a high volatile acidity also lowers it.

result.title: The result
result.content: Here you will see the predicted quality. It does not have to be a whole number: the network may say, for example, 5.6. If you used a row without changing it, you will also see the real score and the error.

end.title: Your turn
end.content: Choose a wine, predict its quality and then raise the alcohol to see how the prediction changes. You can open this guide again whenever you like with the Guide button.

model.title: The model
model.content: This is the model card: what it detects, what it receives and what it returns. It is an already trained model: here it is only used, not trained.

explain-about.title: How it is explained
explain-about.content: This box sums up how the explainability is computed: the image is split into pieces, they are covered in many different combinations and we look at how much the result changes. That way we know which areas weighed the most.

webcam.title: Real-time recognition
webcam.content: Here you see the camera image with what the model detects drawn on top, up to twenty times per second.

webcam-controls.title: The camera controls
webcam-controls.content: With the switch you turn on the webcam; the browser will ask for permission the first time. With the drop-down you choose the camera, if you have several. The photo camera button downloads a capture and the last one puts the camera in full screen.

device-info.title: Device information
device-info.content: Here you have the details of your camera, your browser and your screen, and how the detection is going: how many predictions per second it makes and how long each one takes.

image.title: Recognition in images
image.content: If you do not have a camera, drag a photo here or choose it from your computer: the model processes it and draws on top what it detects.

explain.title: Explainability
explain.content: After processing a photo, here you can compute its explanation: a heat map on the image that marks which areas weighed the most in what the model detected.

end.title: Your turn
end.content: Turn on the webcam or upload a photo and see what the model detects. You can open this guide again whenever you like with the Guide button.

intro.title: Face detection
intro.content: On this page, the MediaPipe Face Detector model finds the faces in a photo or in the camera, up to four at a time, and marks six key points on each one: the eyes, the nose, the mouth and the ears. I will explain what each thing is, step by step. You can move on with Next, go back, mute the voice or let the guide move on by itself.

webcam.title: Real-time recognition
webcam.content: When you turn on the camera you will see the key points of your face with their names on top of it, in real time. The image is shown as in a mirror.

end.title: Your turn
end.content: Turn on the webcam, turn your head or cover part of your face and see when it stops finding it. You can open this guide again whenever you like with the Guide button.

intro.title: Face mesh
intro.content: On this page, the MediaPipe Face Mesh model finds the faces in a photo or in the camera, up to four at a time, and places hundreds of points on each one, forming a three-dimensional mesh of its surface. I will explain what each thing is, step by step. You can move on with Next, go back, mute the voice or let the guide move on by itself.

webcam.title: Real-time recognition
webcam.content: When you turn on the camera you will see the mesh of points on top of your face, following your expressions in real time. The image is shown as in a mirror.

end.title: Your turn
end.content: Turn on the webcam, open your mouth, wink or raise your eyebrows and see how the mesh follows each expression. You can open this guide again whenever you like with the Guide button.

intro.title: Joint detector
intro.content: On this page, the MoveNet model estimates the posture of the body: up to five people at a time, with seventeen points each, such as the eyes, the ears, the shoulders, the elbows, the wrists, the hips, the knees and the ankles. I will explain what each thing is, step by step. You can move on with Next, go back, mute the voice or let the guide move on by itself.

webcam.title: Real-time recognition
webcam.content: When you turn on the camera you will see the points of each person joined by lines, like a skeleton that moves with you. Step back a little so that your whole body is visible.

end.title: Your turn
end.content: Turn on the webcam, step back until your whole body is visible and move your arms and legs. You can open this guide again whenever you like with the Guide button.

intro.title: Object detector
intro.content: On this page, the COCO-SSD model finds objects in a photo or in the camera: it draws a box around them and says what they are and how confident it is. It recognises eighty classes from the COCO data set, such as people, animals, vehicles, food or furniture. I will explain what each thing is, step by step. You can move on with Next, go back, mute the voice or let the guide move on by itself.

webcam.title: Real-time recognition
webcam.content: When you turn on the camera you will see a box around each object it recognises, with its name and the percentage of confidence.

end.title: Your turn
end.content: Turn on the webcam and hold up a cup, a bottle, a book or your phone: see what it recognises and how confident it is. You can open this guide again whenever you like with the Guide button.

intro.title: Facial expressions
intro.content: On this page, face-api, a set of several neural networks, finds the faces in a photo or in the camera and estimates for each one its approximate age and its expression: neutral, happy, sad, angry, fearful, disgusted or surprised. I will explain what each thing is, step by step. You can move on with Next, go back, mute the voice or let the guide move on by itself.

webcam.title: Real-time recognition
webcam.content: When you turn on the camera you will see a box around each face with its estimated age and how much its expression looks like each emotion.

end.title: Your turn
end.content: Turn on the webcam and try smiling, looking surprised or angry: see how the percentages of each expression change. You can open this guide again whenever you like with the Guide button.

intro.title: Sign language
intro.content: On this page, a neural network finds your hand and twenty-one points on its fingers and joints; then another program compares the position of the fingers with the letters of the fingerspelling alphabet: Spanish Sign Language if the application is in Spanish, and American Sign Language in the other languages. I will explain what each thing is, step by step. You can move on with Next, go back, mute the voice or let the guide move on by itself.

webcam.title: Real-time recognition
webcam.content: When you turn on the camera you will see the points of your hand and the letter it recognises. Hold your hand facing the camera, well lit and fully inside the image.

end.title: Your turn
end.content: Turn on the webcam, look at the image with the alphabet in the model card and try to form several letters with your hand. You can open this guide again whenever you like with the Guide button.

model.title: The model
model.content: This is the model card: which images it was trained with, what it receives and which classes it can recognise.

model-summary.title: Model summary
model-summary.content: This button opens the summary of the network: its layers, how many neurons each one has and how many parameters, which are the weights it adjusted during training.

explain-about.title: How it is explained
explain-about.content: This box sums up the method used to explain the predictions. LRP goes back through the network and shares out the decision down to the pixels; SHAP covers pieces of the image in many combinations and looks at how much the result changes.

examples.title: Example images
examples.content: Press any of these images to classify it: the result appears further down.

test-images.title: Test images
test-images.content: With this button you load the test images, the ones the network did not see during training. Then, in this same place, you choose any of them to classify it and compare the prediction with its real class.

upload.title: Upload an image
upload.content: You can also drag an image of your own here, or choose it from your computer, and press the button to classify it.

draw.title: Draw
draw.content: Or draw here with the mouse or your finger and press the button to classify your drawing. It is reduced to 28 by 28 pixels, like the images the network was trained with.

result.title: The result
result.content: Here you will see the image that was classified and, next to it, the probability of each class. The highest one is the prediction.

explain.title: Explainability
explain.content: After classifying, here you compute a heat map on the image that marks which pixels weighed the most in the decision of the network.

end.title: Your turn
end.content: Classify an example, upload an image of your own and look at the explainability to see what the network paid attention to. You can open this guide again whenever you like with the Guide button.

intro.title: Digit recognition
intro.content: On this page, a convolutional neural network that has already been trained recognises handwritten numbers from 0 to 9. I will explain what each thing is, step by step. You can move on with Next, go back, mute the voice or let the guide move on by itself.

model.title: The model
model.content: The network was trained with MNIST, a collection of 70,000 handwritten digits, 60,000 for training and 10,000 for testing, in greyscale images of 28 by 28 pixels. It is one of the most used data sets to get started with machine learning.

examples.title: Example images
examples.content: Press any of these digits to classify it: the result appears further down.

draw.title: Draw a number
draw.content: Draw a number from 0 to 9 here with the mouse or your finger and press the button to classify it. Your drawing is reduced to 28 by 28 pixels, like the MNIST ones, so draw it big and centred.

result.title: The result
result.content: Here you will see the image the network saw and the probability of each digit. The highest one is the prediction. If you classify a test image, you will also see which digit it really was.

explain.title: Explainability with LRP
explain.content: After classifying, here you compute a heat map with LRP, which shares out the decision of the network backwards, layer by layer, down to the pixels: you will see which strokes of the drawing weighed the most.

end.title: Your turn
end.content: Draw a number your own way, for example a seven with a cross bar or a one with a base, and see whether the network recognises it and what it paid attention to. You can open this guide again whenever you like with the Guide button.

intro.title: Japanese characters
intro.content: On this page, a convolutional neural network that has already been trained recognises ten Japanese characters of the hiragana syllabary handwritten in kuzushiji, the cursive script used in Japan for centuries. I will explain what each thing is, step by step. You can move on with Next, go back, mute the voice or let the guide move on by itself.

model.title: The model
model.content: The network was trained with Kuzushiji-MNIST: images of 28 by 28 pixels, like the MNIST ones, but with characters instead of digits. It is harder than MNIST, because the same character can be written in very different ways.

examples.title: Example images
examples.content: Press any of these characters to classify it: the result appears further down.

draw.title: Draw a character
draw.content: Draw one of the ten characters here with the mouse or your finger and press the button to classify it. Bear in mind that the network learned the old cursive script, which does not always look like today's hiragana.

result.title: The result
result.content: Here you will see the image the network saw and the probability of each character. The highest one is the prediction. If you classify a test image, you will also see which character it really was.

explain.title: Explainability with LRP
explain.content: After classifying, here you compute a heat map with LRP, which shares out the decision of the network backwards, layer by layer, down to the pixels: you will see which strokes weighed the most.

end.title: Your turn
end.content: Load the test images and compare several ways of writing the same character: you will see the network get it right even with very different strokes. You can open this guide again whenever you like with the Guide button.

intro.title: Image classification
intro.content: On this page, MobileNet, a convolutional neural network designed for mobile phones, recognises what appears in a photo among a thousand categories: animals, objects, vehicles, food and much more. I will explain what each thing is, step by step. You can move on with Next, go back, mute the voice or let the guide move on by itself.

model.title: The model
model.content: It is MobileNet, trained with ImageNet, more than a million photos of a thousand categories. It receives colour images of 224 by 224 pixels.

examples.title: Example images
examples.content: Press any of these photos to classify it: the result appears further down.

upload.title: Upload an image
upload.content: Drag a photo of your own here, or choose it from your computer, and press the button to classify it. It works better if what you want to recognise fills almost the whole photo.

result.title: The result
result.content: Here you will see the photo the network saw and the most likely categories, from highest to lowest. With a thousand categories, it is normal for it to hesitate between several similar ones, such as two breeds of dog.

explain.title: Explainability with SHAP
explain.content: After classifying, here you compute a heat map with SHAP: the photo is split into pieces, they are covered in many combinations and we look at how much the prediction changes. That way you see which areas of the photo weighed the most.

end.title: Your turn
end.content: Upload a photo of something near you and see whether the network recognises it and what it paid attention to. You can open this guide again whenever you like with the Guide button.
